definition: Indexed grammars are a generalization of context-free grammars in that nonterminals are equipped with lists of flags, or index symbols.
details: The language produced by an indexed grammar is called an indexed language.

explainer.lead: Indexed grammars generalize context-free grammars by equipping nonterminals with lists of flags, or index symbols. They matter because the languages they produce form a class useful beyond context-free power.

tiers.eli5: It's a set of grammar rules where each symbol can carry a little list of notes that shapes what it can turn into.
tiers.practitioner: Language engineers use them to describe nonlocal constraints that plain context-free grammars miss. A pitfall is complexity: they exceed context-free power and require nested stack machinery to parse.
tiers.paperLevel: A generalization of context-free grammars in which nonterminals carry lists of index symbols; the language produced is called an indexed language.

explainer.example: A grammar whose nonterminal carries an index list distinguishes agreement patterns that a plain context-free grammar cannot express.
